title: Small things up close
hook: a leaf, an insect, frost: the world gets bigger the closer you look

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was one tree, and your line was something ordinary becomes someone you visit. Today, closer still: past the branch, to the leaf.

A frosted car window on a cold morning. The usual move is to scrape it off and drive. But lean in first, and the frost isn't a white smear at all. It's ferns. Feathers. Tiny branching forests, grown in the dark while you slept. The same goes for the veins on a leaf, the legs of a beetle, the rings of a cut onion. Awe is often filed under big things: mountains, oceans, stars. Today it goes the other way. The world gets bigger the closer you look.
screen: `FROST ON A WINDOW.` → `FERNS, FEATHERS, FORESTS.` → `BIGGER THE CLOSER YOU LOOK.`

segments.voice: First, a poet's grain of sand. William Blake, the English poet, opens his poem Auguries of Innocence with two lines: "To see a World in a Grain of Sand / And a Heaven in a Wild Flower." He isn't saying sand is pretty. He's saying the whole is folded into the very small, if you have eyes for it. Second, a teacher's flowers. In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus points his listeners to the plants at their feet: "Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin." Then he says that Solomon, in all his glory, was not dressed like one of these. A king's robes, outshone by a wild flower. The word is consider. Not glance: stay with it. Third, why small works. Something huge can overwhelm you; you stand back from it. Something small invites you in. You have to bend down, slow down, get quiet, and that posture, low and close and still, is half the practice already. Fourth, what it changes. Spend a minute with the veins of one leaf, and a whole tree is never quite a green blur again. The detail stays with you. And small things are everywhere: on the windowsill, in the sidewalk crack, on the back of your own hand. You don't need a trip to find awe. You need to bend down.
screen: `BLAKE: A WORLD IN A GRAIN OF SAND.` · `MATTHEW: CONSIDER THE LILIES.` · `SMALL THINGS INVITE YOU IN.` · `YOU DON'T NEED A TRIP. JUST BEND DOWN.` · then, large: `CONSIDER.`

segments.voice: Bring one small thing close, a leaf, a crumb, a drop of water on a glass, the back of your own hand, and look at its edges, then its surface, then the lines and grains and tiny colors inside it. When your mind wanders, come back to one detail. If you pray, let this be a way of attending to what's made; if you don't, simply look.
Solomon. The king Jesus named when pointing to the lilies of the field, outshone by a wild flower: bend down, look long, and the small thing opens. Today's word.
Your line: up close. Even a crumb has edges worth a second look. Day one thousand thirty-eight, done.

howItsDone: Poets, naturalists and contemplatives in several settings practice close looking at small living things; Blake's Auguries of Innocence and Jesus's words about the lilies in Matthew 6 are two texts that point the eye downward.

chat.says: Isn't awe for big things, like mountains and oceans?
options: Small things work too: bend down and look long, and a leaf or frost opens up.
Mostly, yes; small things are pretty, but real awe needs something huge and far away.
Only if you study them under a microscope, the way a scientist would.
chat.meaning: Something small invites you in. Blake saw a world in a grain of sand, and Jesus told his listeners to consider the lilies.
